title: One Nation says it would cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% under ‘tough stance’
summary:
Pauline Hanson opens new war of words on immigration as foreign minister Penny Wong accuses populist party of ‘dividing Australians’

  • Get our

blocks.text: One Nation has vowed to cut Australia’s refugee intake by 90% and scrap the permanent parent visa program under its latest hardline plan to slash migration.
Pauline Hanson announced the policy on Tuesday labelling it a “tough” approach to migration.
The rightwing party said if it held power it would cut the refugee program from 20,000 places per year to 2,000 and claimed Australia would still remain above the OECD average for places per capita.
One Nation’s push would end Australia’s status as one of the most generous refugee programs behind Canada.
“The cost [to] … the taxpayer is enormous. The cost is, on average, about $500,000 a year in a lifetime of expenditure per person in the country,” Hanson told reporters.

“We’ve got to take a tough stance on this. My concern is for these people out there … that are doing it tough. You don’t bring more people into the country if they cannot fund their own bed or hospital beds.”

Hanson claimed her plan would save the budget more than $140bn over 10 years. Migrants from countries on the Albanese government’s “do not travel” list, including Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Somalia, would still be banned from entering the country.

One Nation says analysis based on Treasury modelling, adjusted for inflation, found the lifetime cost of a humanitarian entrant was $523,000. Treasury modelling done in December 2021 found the cost was $400,000 with 90% of it borne by the federal government.
Labor has committed to retaining the refugee intake at 20,000 per year while the Coalition has promised to halve it to 10,000.

The foreign minister, Penny Wong, accused One Nation of trying to divide the country. She said Australia had the right balance and questioned Hanson’s claim that Australia would remain above the OECD average under the minor party’s plan.

“I don’t accept those figures and I find when Ms Hanson speaks, you always have to check what is actually being said. There are countries which take more refugees, there are countries which take fewer. We think this [20,000 per year] is the right balance,” Wong said.

“We have unprecedented people movement around the world. We have displacement of more human beings than at any time since world war II. We make a very small contribution to that by our refugee intake.”
Wong said it was “more of the same” from One Nation.
“I know that they think dividing Australians is the best response to the politics of the time,” the Labor frontbencher said. “I take a different view.”
Other nations including the US and Canada have tightened their migration programs in recent years with Canada reducing its parent visa program.
Hanson said One Nation was not barring migrant parents from moving to Australia, but they would have to be sponsored, or could visit their families on temporary visas.
“We’re not saying parents can’t come out … [but] they will actually be sponsored by the families not the taxpayers.”
